phase1.explanation:
Every field and method you've written so far has belonged to individual objects — [[term:static]] members flip that: [[key:they belong to the CLASS itself, with exactly one shared copy, no matter how many objects you create]].

Watch `staticCount` in the example: every single `Counter` object increments the SAME shared number, while `instanceCount` resets fresh for each object. That's the core distinction — [[key:instance variables are per-object, static variables are shared across every object of that class]].

Static methods follow the same rule, with a real consequence: [[warn:a static method can't directly touch instance variables]], because a static method isn't attached to any particular object — there's no `this` to reach into. You call a static method on the class itself, `Counter.displayStatic()`, never needing an object at all.

A [[term:static block]] — the `static { ... }` you see at the top of the example — runs exactly once, the very first time the class gets loaded, before even `main()` starts. It's mainly there for one-time setup work.

And `static final` together is the standard way to write a real constant — `static final double PI = 3.14159;` — [[key:one shared value, and static final means it can never change]]. The entire `Math` class, in fact, is built almost entirely out of static methods — that's exactly why you never need a `Math` object to call `Math.sqrt(16)`.

phase2.errorMessage:
Counter.java:8: error: non-static variable instanceValue cannot be referenced from a static context
        instanceValue = 10;  // ERROR!
        ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:A static method has no attached object, so it has no way to reach instanceValue]] — instance variables only exist once an object has actually been created, and a static method can be called with zero objects in existence at all.

[[key:There are really three honest ways to fix this]]: make `instanceValue` static too, if it genuinely should be shared across every object; access it through a specific object reference (`someCounter.instanceValue`) instead of directly; or simply don't try to touch instance state from a static method at all. [[key:The rule to remember is simple]]: a static context can only directly reach other static members.

mcq.question:
Why can't a static method directly access an instance variable?

A) Instance variables are always private
B) A static method isn't tied to any specific object, so there's no instance to read the variable from
C) Static methods run before instance variables are created in memory
D) This restriction doesn't actually exist

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a Student class with:
• Instance fields: name (String), grade (int)
• Static field: schoolName (String) — shared by all students
• Static method: setSchoolName(String name) — sets the school name
• Constructor: sets name and grade
• Method: displayInfo() — prints all info

In main, create 3 students, set school name once, and display all.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: a static block doesn't necessarily run the moment your program starts — it runs the first time that specific class actually gets loaded by the JVM, which in a big program might be well after main() begins, whenever something first references that class.
